name: MM Proposition I
use: Perfect capital markets: firm value does not depend on capital structure.

vars.meaning: value of the same firm without debt
market values of equity and debt

pitfall: Equity value = V_U − D, not the PV of equity cash flows at r_U.
example:
Task type: the firm changes its debt (perfect markets) – firm value stays, find the new equity value.
Unlevered firm worth V_U = 1,000; it borrows D = 400 and pays it out to shareholders
V_L = 1,000 still → equity E = 1,000 − 400 = 600

name: Average cost stays unchanged
use: Check any levered return calculation against the unlevered cost.

vars.meaning: market values of equity and debt

example:
Task type: you computed r_E after a leverage change – check that the average still equals r_U.
r_U = 10%, r_D = 5%, E = 600, D = 400 → r_E = 13.33% (MM II)
0.6 × 13.33% + 0.4 × 5% = 8% + 2% = 10% = r_U ✓

name: Homemade leverage
formula: \begin{aligned} &\text{replicate } x\% \text{ of the levered equity } E\text{:} \\[4pt] &\text{buy } x\% \text{ of } U \text{ and borrow } x\% \text{ of } D \end{aligned}
use: Arbitrage argument behind MM I (investors borrow at the firm's rate).

vars.meaning: share of the levered firm you want to own
debt of the levered firm (you borrow at the same rate)

example:
Task type: show that investors can copy the firm's leverage themselves, so leverage cannot add value.
Levered firm: E = 600, D = 400; unlevered twin U worth 1,000
Copy 10% of E: buy 10% of U (100) and borrow 10% of D (40) → own money 60 = 10% of E
Payoff: 10% of the firm's cash flow minus 10% of the interest – the same as holding 10% of E
